newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE-Ousted general sets sights on Colombia presidency.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Ousted general sets sights on Colombia presidency.

text.p: Tough-talking Gen. Harold Bedoya is putting his unceremonious dismissal as Colombia's armed forces chief behind him and pushing for promotion -- to the presidency.

In an interview with Reuters, he outlined his fledgling plans for what he termed a "popular and national" government that would grant more powers to the state and could curtail individual rights of citizens in a bid to crush the country's powerful leftist guerrilla groups.

Bedoya, 58, hinted that if he is elected in May 1998 he would seek to introduce sweeping changes that could extend his period in office or even open the way to his re-election. Under the present constitution a president serves for a non-renewable four-year term.

"I will be a good president. ... Mine will be a national movement that represents all Colombians, rich and poor," he said in his impromptu campaign office in northern Bogota. "It will be a government that seeks to recover national dignity and values based around the fundamental nucleus of the nation, which is the family."

But the square-jawed military hawk rejected suggestions he wanted to create an authoritarian, populist and nationalist government, saying he would rule without "distinction of class or ideology" in a way that would be "popular for everybody."

Bedoya headed the military for just 8-1/2 months before a series of public disagreements over President Ernesto Samper's plans to launch new talks to end Colombia's three-decade rebel uprising ended in his firing in late July.
LITTLE SUCCESS FOR MILITARY IN POLITICS

The army has little history of direct involvement in politics and retired officers who, like Bedoya, have ventured into the political arena have been obliterated by a system where regional power-brokers guarantee block votes for the traditional Liberal and Conservative parties in return for a wide array of favours and kickbacks.

But in three early polls, the ousted general, due to formally register his presidential candidacy in the next few weeks, is already emerging as a leading contender, with about 40 percent of voter support. That puts him level or even ahead of his main rivals, former Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, widely seen as Samper's straw man, and former Chief Prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso, seen by many as a puppet of Washington.

Bedoya enjoys support from the right wings of both the ruling Liberal and opposition Conservative parties and has a gaggle of high-profile female admirers, including top models, actresses and the director of the National Theatre. A central plank of his platform, still on the drawing board, is likely to be a blueprint for the military defeat of the rebel armies, now embarked on one of their bloodiest offensives in years.

Bedoya, who was trained at the U.S. School of the Americas and has been accused by human rights group of sponsoring right-wing death squads, has firmly resisted Samper's plans for no-holds-barred talks with the rebels. "I want those who commit crimes to have to respond for them ... the state cannot afford to be weakened by handing over territory or sovereignty (to the guerrillas)," he said.
GREATER SPENDING ON WAR EFFORT

In order to blast the rebels into submission he said he would "strengthen state institutions," including the armed forces -- an indication that he would earmark a greater share of the budget for the war effort even as civilian politicians demand more restraint and efficiency in defence spending.
Hand-in-hand with the military strategy, Bedoya contemplates the wider use of emergency powers to give security forces more clout in their anti-guerrilla campaign.

Political analysts charge such a move could polarise the country if individual rights are partially suspended by curfews, temporary imposition of martial law and appointment of military rulers in areas dominated by the guerrillas.
Under the guise of fortifying state institutions, the general also hinted that once in office he may engineer what would undoubtedly be a highly controversial power-grab.

"(Re-election) will be a theme for discussion in the course of my government," he said. "I think if Colombia sees the country is recovering then people will want to see the government prolonged. But that's a democratic process."

Coupled with his fervent anti-guerrilla stance, Bedoya has promised a "crusade" against the kind of deep-rooted political corruption exposed by allegations that Samper financed his 1994 election campaign with donations from the Cali drug mob.
"The narco-scandal was a detonator but the problems had been brewing for 10 or 15 years," he said.

In comments sure to be welcomed by U.S. anti-drug agents, with whom he enjoys warm personal relations, he said he would push hard for drug cartel capos to be extradited to stand trial in U.S. courts and is open to the possibility of reopening investigations into Samper's role in the drug-funding scandal.

Bedoya still seems ill-at-ease in a jacket and tie after 42 years in uniform, but he is confident the same charisma that won him wide respect in the ranks as a soldier's soldier will translate into votes for the nation's top job.
